title: Detecting and Summarizing Action Items in Multi-Party Dialogue
research_question: Can action items in natural multi-party meetings be detected as structured multi-utterance commitments and summarized into useful task and timeframe information under both manual-transcript and speech-recognition conditions?
methodology: The authors annotate 18 natural ICSI research-group meetings using four action-item dialogue-act classes: Description, Timeframe, Owner, and Agreement. Four SVM classifiers identify these classes and a higher-level classifier combines their labels and confidences over a ten-utterance context window; evaluation uses leave-one-meeting-out cross-validation and compares structured detection with a flat binary baseline on manual transcripts, 1-best ASR, and word confusion networks. For summarization, a rule-based semantic parser generates candidate task-description and timeframe phrases, which are ranked using SVM regression and lexical, syntactic, semantic, temporal, and acoustic features.

key_findings.finding: The structured detector outperforms the flat detector on manual transcripts, reaching overlap-based F1 of 0.45 versus 0.35 for the flat approach.

Automatic speech recognition reduces action-item detection performance substantially; the structured overlap F1 falls from 0.45 on manual transcripts to 0.36 on 1-best ASR, with word confusion networks recovering only a small amount to 0.37.

Timeframe summarization benefits from semantic and temporal features, with the best reported automatic configuration reaching F1 0.51 compared with 0.31 for a TIMEX-only baseline and 0.39 for an entire-utterance baseline.
Task-description summarization remains difficult: semantic features can raise precision, but the evaluated candidate-ranking systems do not exceed the entire-utterance description baseline in F1.

The action-item annotations are sparse and moderately to substantially reproducible, with only about 1.4% of utterances receiving any action-item class and pairwise kappa values ranging from 0.64 to 0.78.

limitations: The study uses 18 meetings from the ICSI Meeting Corpus, so organizational and domain diversity is limited.
Action-item utterances are very sparse, with only about 1.4% of utterances carrying any of the four action-item labels.
ASR errors cause substantial degradation relative to manual transcripts.
The structured detector's advantage over the flat detector is not statistically significant in the reported ASR conditions.
Owner identity extraction is explicitly left outside the summarization experiment even though Owner is annotated for detection.
Task descriptions can span multiple utterances, while the summarizer selects material from a single acoustically segmented utterance.
Sentence and utterance segmentation errors limit semantic parsing and description extraction.
The paper does not report release of the task-specific annotations or complete custom implementation as reproducibility artifacts.
raw_claims: The paper treats action items as public commitments to carry out tasks rather than merely as sentences mentioning future activity.
The annotation scheme distinguishes Description, Timeframe, Owner, and Agreement utterances.
Eighteen natural ICSI meetings are used in the experiments.
Pairwise annotation kappa values range from 0.64 to 0.78.
Only about 1.4% of meeting utterances receive at least one action-item label.
Four independent SVM classifiers feed a higher-level detector that examines a ten-utterance context.
Structured detection performs better than flat detection on manual transcripts.
ASR degrades both structured and flat action-item detection.
Word confusion networks provide only a small improvement over 1-best ASR in the reported detection results.
Semantic and TIMEX features substantially improve timeframe extraction.
The task-description extractor does not outperform using the full utterance as the description baseline.
The authors note that useful summaries may need information combined across multiple utterances.
